title: Marble Run: Gravity's Roller Coaster

body.heading: A roller coaster for one marble
paragraphs: Every roller coaster on Earth runs on one engine: gravity. No batteries, no motor — just height and the pull of the Earth. Your marble run is a pocket roller coaster: you give the marble height, and gravity does the rest.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The start gate — the highest point, where the marble waits full of promise. The ramps — slanted tubes and channels that guide the fall. The turns — cups or curved tubes that catch the marble and send it a new way. The supports — books and boxes holding everything up. The finish bowl — a cup or box that catches the marble at the bottom.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: Cardboard tubes (kitchen-roll and wrapping-paper tubes), cardboard strips, a cereal box, tape, safety scissors, books and boxes for supports, a bowl or cup for the finish, and one marble — plus a grown-up for cutting and tower safety.

paragraphs: Step 1 — Plan the drop. Choose your wall or tower of books. A good run zigzags: down one ramp, turn, down the next, so the marble travels far without falling too fast.
Step 2 — Build the first ramp. Tape a tube or folded cardboard channel at a gentle slant — steep enough to roll, gentle enough to control. Rest its low end above the first turn.
Step 3 — Add turns and more ramps. Each ramp must start a little lower than the one above ended — a marble can never roll higher than where it started without a push. Test after every piece you add.

Step 4 — The grand run. Drop the marble at the start gate and watch: it speeds up on the steeps, slows on the shallows, and rattles around the turns into the finish bowl. If it flies off, engineers call that data — soften that ramp and test again.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: At the top, the marble holds potential energy — stored energy from being high up. As it rolls down, that energy turns into movement. Steeper ramps trade height for speed faster; gentle ramps trade slowly. Friction — the rubbing between marble and track — steals a little energy the whole way, which is why the marble can never climb higher than its start.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why can the marble never roll UP to a point higher than the start gate?
2. Where on your run is the marble moving fastest? How can you tell — and how could you slow it down there?

takeaway: A marble run trades height for speed: gravity turns stored energy at the top into movement all the way down, and friction makes sure the marble never climbs higher than it started.
materials: Cereal box or stiff card for channels
supervision: A grown-up helps with cutting and checks tall towers are stable before the first run.
safetyNotes: Marbles are a choking hazard — this build is for children 5 and up, and marbles must be counted out and counted back into a closed box, away from toddlers and pets.
Tape runs to a wall only with a grown-up's permission, on a surface they approve — paint and wallpaper can peel.
Keep towers below shoulder height and never lean over a run from above; rebuild wobbly supports instead of holding them during a run.
screenFreeExtension: Two-marble race day: build a second short ramp next to the finish bowl, race marbles of different sizes, and keep a chalk tally of which size wins most often.
